ocar.opportunity: How external and internal sensory inputs select among possible motor and neuroendocrine paths is a basic problem in circuit organization, and Drosophila larva feeding is tractable for whole-CNS synaptic mapping plus behavior.
ocar.challenge: Synaptic-resolution maps of entire nervous systems remain rare, so the central architecture that routes enteric, pharyngeal, and external sensory input onto feeding motor and endocrine outputs was largely unknown.
ocar.action: Miroschnikow, Schlegel, Schoofs, Hückesfeld, Li, Schneider-Mizell, Fetter, Truman, Cardona, and Pankratz reconstruct from a whole-CNS electron-microscopy volume the synaptic map of input and output neurons that underlie larval food intake, posted on bioRxiv (2018).
ocar.resolution: Sensory axons converge onto seven topographic synaptic compartments in the subesophageal zone. Monosynaptic connections, mostly enteric, cover overlapping motor and endocrine targets and form an elemental feeding circuit, while distinct polysynaptic routes overlay that reflex arc; a different set of compartments innervates the mushroom-body calyx.
ocar.future_work: The authors analogize sparse somatosensory monosynaptic reflexes to C. elegans head (versus body) circuits and cite unpublished ventral-nerve-cord data; they frame the architecture as a template for feeding reflexes and other instinctive behaviors rather than a completed functional census.

summaries.beginner: This team traces feeding-related neurons in a fruit-fly larva brain from electron-microscope pictures. Direct sensory-to-motor shortcuts and longer multi-step paths both land on the same swallowing and hormone-output cells.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2018), Miroschnikow and colleagues reconstruct a synaptic feeding connectome from a Drosophila larva whole-CNS EM volume. Enteric, pharyngeal, and external sensory neurons terminate in seven presynaptic compartments of the subesophageal zone, a region they compare to the vertebrate brainstem. Outputs include pharyngeal motor neurons, serotonergic modulators, and neuroendocrine cells targeting the ring gland. Most monosynaptic links are enteric and cannot be subdivided further; somatosensory monosynaptic reflexes onto mouth-hook and head-tilt motor neurons are few. A separate sensory set reaches the mushroom-body calyx.
summaries.advanced: The selected extract is a July 2018 bioRxiv preprint, not a later journal version. “Vast majority” of elemental-circuit inputs are described as enteric without a count in this extract. The claim of fewer monosynaptic reflexes in the larval VNC is explicitly unpublished (Ohyama et al., 2015). Functional assignment of compartments is anatomical (modality and peripheral origin), not a full activity map.

plain_language_summary: This team traces feeding-related neurons in a fruit-fly larva brain from electron-microscope pictures. Direct sensory-to-motor shortcuts and longer multi-step paths both land on the same swallowing and hormone-output cells.

ocar.opportunity: A complexity measure that vanishes for fully random and fully ordered graphs could identify which wiring features make a real neuronal network “complex” and whether those features have physiological meaning.
ocar.challenge: There is no universally accepted quantification of network complexity, and it is unclear which substructures of the C. elegans connectome generate excess complexity beyond what the degree sequence would predict.
ocar.action: Kunert-Graf, Sakhanenko, and Galas apply the Sakhanenko–Galas information-theoretic measure Ψ to the undirected binary gap-junction network of the C. elegans somatic nervous system in Entropy (2017), then iteratively delete the connections whose removal most reduces complexity.
ocar.resolution: The intact gap-junction graph is much more complex than degree-matched random graphs; that excess is concentrated in a small set of connections involving command interneurons that overlap the synaptic network’s previously identified rich club. After those edges are removed, complexity falls below the random-graph baseline, supporting a picture of a low-complexity backbone whose symmetry is broken by those neurons.
ocar.future_work: The authors note that the rich club is defined on the chemical-synapse graph, not gap junctions; Ψ is pairwise and unweighted; betweenness changes little (about 1.29× to 1.22× after 40 deletions) while complexity drops sharply. They flag directed synapses, edge weights, higher-order measures, and other complexity definitions as next steps.

summaries.beginner: The worm C. elegans has a complete map of electrical junctions among its neurons. This paper shows that a few command cells make that map far more complex than a random network with the same number of links, and that removing those links makes it simpler than random.
summaries.intermediate: In Entropy (2017), Kunert-Graf, Sakhanenko, and Galas quantify complexity of the C. elegans somatic gap-junction connectome with the Kolmogorov-inspired measure Ψ of Sakhanenko and Galas. Excess complexity relative to degree-preserving random graphs traces to connections of command interneurons, including cells whose chemical-synapse rich-club membership was previously reported. Iterative deletion of complexity-causing edges leaves a network less complex than random. Average betweenness centrality falls only modestly over 40 deletions (factor ~1.29 to ~1.22 versus random), so complexity here is not a restatement of betweenness. The authors cite AVAL/R and AVBL/R ablation phenotypes as physiological context for command interneurons.
summaries.advanced: Analysis is restricted to an undirected, unweighted gap-junction graph among 302 neurons; chemical synapses and gap-junction multiplicity are omitted. “Rich club” is imported from the synaptic network. Ψ sums pairwise mutual information and may miss higher-order structure. There is no single accepted complexity definition; the authors treat their deconstruction as a method, not a unique inventory of important edges.

plain_language_summary: The worm C. elegans has a complete map of electrical junctions among its neurons. This paper shows that a few command cells make that map far more complex than a random network with the same number of links, and that removing those links makes it simpler than random.

ocar.opportunity: Identifying how neurons are wired is required both to understand circuit computation and because aberrant wiring is implicated in some neurodevelopmental disorders.
ocar.challenge: No single tracing method answers every question: model systems differ in cell number and physiology, and each anatomical technique has distinct strengths and limits.
ocar.action: Lee, Huang, De La Cruz, Callejas, and Lois review in Fly (2017) methods then available to investigate nervous-system structure and connectivity, comparing C. elegans, Drosophila, and mouse as experimental systems.
ocar.resolution: They argue that method choice should follow the scientific question. Electron microscopy is described as impractical for watching synapses change over time or after genetic perturbation, but valuable for systems-level models when resources allow. Drosophila is presented as a middle ground: far fewer neurons than mouse, more sophisticated behavior than C. elegans, and genetic tools that support cellular-level circuit maps.
ocar.future_work: The review points readers to a comparison table of methods rather than a new dataset; remaining obstacles are those of the individual techniques surveyed, not a single experimental gap the authors close here.

summaries.beginner: This review surveys ways to figure out which brain cells connect to which. The authors say you should pick the method based on the question: electron microscopy is great for a wiring snapshot, not for watching synapses change.
summaries.intermediate: In Fly (2017), Lee and colleagues review connectomics-oriented methods for mapping structure and connectivity. They contrast C. elegans (fast genetics, limited behavior, no sodium-dependent spikes, difficult electrophysiology), Drosophila (on the order of 100,000 neurons, sophisticated genetics, some circuit motifs shared with mammals), and mouse (mammalian conservation, more than 100 million neurons). The conclusion stresses matching method to question: EM is poorly suited to time-resolved or genetically induced synaptic change but, when resources allow, is valuable for systems-level models.
summaries.advanced: This is a methods review with a comparison table (Table 1) that is not reproduced in the selected extract. The C. elegans neuron count in the introduction (“just over 1000”) is the authors’ wording and does not match the canonical 302-neuron census; treat it as a review-level approximation, not a new count. Strengths and limitations of individual techniques should be checked against Table 1 and the primary papers cited.

plain_language_summary: This review surveys ways to figure out which brain cells connect to which. The authors say you should pick the method based on the question: electron microscopy is great for a wiring snapshot, not for watching synapses change.

ocar.opportunity: Neuronal boundary detection on serial-section EM images is the first step of a common anisotropic reconstruction pipeline and would benefit from multi-scale context that can resolve both thin and thick membranes.
ocar.challenge: Detectors must find filament-like thin and blob-like thick membranes while suppressing ambiguous intracellular structure; isolated pixel-wise decisions leave gaps and false intracellular boundaries.
ocar.action: Shen, Wang, Jiang, Wang, and Yuille propose multi-stage multi-recursive-input fully convolutional networks (M2FCN) at ICCV (2017): side outputs with different receptive fields from one stage are fed as recursive inputs to the next, trained end-to-end.
ocar.resolution: On the mouse piriform-cortex dataset they plot precision–recall against VD2D and VD2D3D. On the ISBI 2012 Drosophila VNC challenge they report a VRand score of 0.9780, tied with FusionNet and behind PolyMtl (0.9806), ahead of U-Net (0.9727). Watershed on their boundary maps is shown as a segmentation example.
ocar.future_work: The paper focuses on 2D membrane detection for anisotropic serial-section stacks; linking segments across sections into 3D remains outside this architecture. The extract does not report a full leaderboard beyond the tabulated VRand scores.

summaries.beginner: Computers that outline cell membranes in electron-microscope pictures often confuse inner clutter with real walls. This team stacks several network stages that look at the picture at different zoom levels and reports strong scores on two public contests.
summaries.intermediate: At the IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision (2017), Shen and colleagues introduce M2FCN: multi-stage fully convolutional networks whose side outputs, learned at different scales, become recursive inputs to the next stage. The design targets 2D neuronal boundary detection in serial-section EM, motivated as the first step of an anisotropic reconstruction pipeline. They evaluate on mouse piriform cortex and the ISBI 2012 Drosophila first-instar VNC dataset (30 test images). Reported ISBI VRand: M2FCN 0.9780, PolyMtl 0.9806, FusionNet 0.9780, U-Net 0.9727. The extract is the arXiv version (1703.08493v2).
summaries.advanced: VRand 0.9780 is not first on the tabulated board. Evaluation is 2D boundary detection plus watershed examples, not a completed 3D connectome. “Biologically-plausible” comparison to human vision is an analogy, not a neural-circuit claim. Pixel-error versus Rand-split/merge trade-offs should be read from Figure 6 rather than a single score.

plain_language_summary: Computers that outline cell membranes in electron-microscope pictures often confuse inner clutter with real walls. This team stacks several network stages that look at the picture at different zoom levels and reports strong scores on two public contests.

ocar.opportunity: Drosophila larvae have simple eyes (Bolwig organs, about 12 photoreceptors each) yet use vision for navigation, circadian entrainment, and memory, so a complete first-stage wiring diagram could link reduced circuit complexity to diverse behaviors.
ocar.challenge: How Rh5 versus Rh6 photoreceptors, local interneurons, and projection neurons are synaptically organized in the larval optic neuropil, and which transmitters they use, was not fully mapped.
ocar.action: Larderet, Fritsch, Gendre, Neagu-Maier, Fetter, Schneider-Mizell, Truman, Zlatic, Cardona, and Sprecher reconstruct the larval visual circuit from the Ohyama et al. (2015) first-instar ssTEM volume in CATMAID and map transmitters with genetic reagents (eLife, 2017).
ocar.resolution: They report 60 neurons, 12.5 mm of cable, 2090 presynaptic and 4414 postsynaptic sites (134 hours tracing plus 43 hours proofreading). Two PR subtypes create converging pathways they propose for ambient intensity versus temporal change; stratified LON organization is compared to adult fly and vertebrate visual systems. Projection interneurons reach lateral horn and mushroom body.
ocar.future_work: Eight lost 50 nm sections (frames 1103–1112) complicated right-hemisphere completeness, with contralateral homologs used to validate gap crossings. Seven tiny fragments remain unattached. The authors call for behavior and physiology to test the Rh6–VLN versus Rh5–VPN functional assignment.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly larvae see with tiny eyes of about a dozen light sensors. This team maps every connection in that first visual hub and suggests one cell type tracks how bright it is while another tracks how brightness is changing.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2017), Larderet and colleagues reconstruct the Drosophila larval visual circuit from a 6-hour-old first-instar ssTEM volume (50 nm sections, 4 nm/pixel) using CATMAID. They find 60 neurons with 12.5 mm of cable, 2090 presynaptic sites, and 4414 postsynaptic sites. Rh5 and Rh6 photoreceptors contact different targets, creating parallel paths hypothesized to encode ambient intensity versus temporal change already in the larval optic neuropil (LON). Dedicated projection interneurons then reach the lateral horn and mushroom body. Reconstruction took 134 hours plus 43 hours of proofreading.
summaries.advanced: Catalog metadata list the venue as bioRxiv; the matching PDF is the eLife article (DOI 10.7554/eLife.28387). Completeness is limited by an eight-section gap and seven unattached fragments (0.018 mm cable, 20 postsynaptic sites). Functional roles of Rh6–VLN versus Rh5–VPN pathways are predictions from connectivity and transmitters, not recordings in this paper. “Complete synaptic wiring diagram of the LON” refers to this volume’s reconstructed neurons, not all developmental stages.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly larvae see with tiny eyes of about a dozen light sensors. This team maps every connection in that first visual hub and suggests one cell type tracks how bright it is while another tracks how brightness is changing.

ocar.opportunity: Complete axonal arbors of long-range projection neurons would show how individual cells route signals across the mammalian brain and would help define projection cell types that bulk tracers mix together.
ocar.challenge: Axons as thin as 100 nm arborize over many millimeters, so few long-range neurons have been reconstructed in their entirety; light scattering, throughput, and 3D disambiguation of crossing fibers all limit whole-brain fluorescence tracing.
ocar.action: Economo, Clack, Lavis, Gerfen, Svoboda, Myers, and Chandrashekar present in eLife (2016) a high-speed two-photon microscope integrated with a tissue vibratome, tissue clearing, and computational tools for large-scale volumes, extending block-face serial two-photon tomography to high-speed 3D imaging.
ocar.resolution: They reconstruct axonal arbors of multiple motor-cortex neurons across a single mouse brain, including five pyramids spanning layers II–VI, with collaterals labeled at high signal-to-noise in white matter, at branch points, and at termini far from the soma.
ocar.future_work: Regions of high labeling density still produce axon crossovers that are ambiguous when fibers are closely apposed in all three dimensions. The platform is demonstrated on a modest number of motor-cortex cells, not a brain-wide census of types.

summaries.beginner: Following a single neuron’s thin axon across a whole mouse brain is usually impractical. This team builds a fast two-photon microscope that shaves and images the brain in 3D and traces several motor-cortex cells all the way to their endings.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2016), Economo and colleagues describe a whole-brain fluorescence platform: high-speed two-photon imaging integrated with a vibratome, clearing, and software for large volumes, extending block-face serial two-photon tomography. They emphasize diffraction-limited, high-NA 3D imaging to disambiguate axons originating from different cells. Demonstration reconstructions include five motor-cortex projection neurons (layers II, V, and VI) with collaterals shown in white matter, at branch points, and at termini in other structures (maximum-intensity projections through 20 µm). Figure 6 overlays complete axonal morphologies on horizontal and sagittal brain outlines.
summaries.advanced: The extract documents five reconstructed motor-cortex neurons, not a dense projectome. Crossover ambiguity in dense labeling remains a reconstruction limit even with 3D imaging. Axon diameter “as small as 100 nm” is a motivation from the abstract, not a measured minimum in the selected figures. This is light-microscopic morphology, not a synaptic connectome.

plain_language_summary: Following a single neuron’s thin axon across a whole mouse brain is usually impractical. This team builds a fast two-photon microscope that shaves and images the brain in 3D and traces several motor-cortex cells all the way to their endings.

ocar.opportunity: The C. elegans connectome, including male mating circuits, offers a global map against which candidate cell-adhesion genes can be compared to ask how synaptic specificity is genetically encoded.
ocar.challenge: How connections are specified during development remains unsolved; male posterior ganglia were too branched for 1970s pencil-and-paper accounting, and EM still struggles on larger brains.
ocar.action: Emmons, in Current Topics in Developmental Biology (2016), reviews the history from Brenner’s choice of C. elegans through White et al. (1986) and the 2012 male mating-circuit reconstruction, then argues for a combinatorial code of neural cell-adhesion proteins.
ocar.resolution: He proposes that comparing genome-wide expression of candidate adhesion proteins with the full set of chemical synapses and gap junctions—rather than one connection at a time—can reveal a logical mapping from labels to wiring, acting stepwise from growth-cone guidance to synapse formation or inhibition.
ocar.future_work: The essay is a program, not a decoded combinatorial table. The wiring code is placed in protein-interaction domains and cis-regulatory expression, which remain to be matched to the connectome at scale.

summaries.beginner: We still do not know which genes tell each worm neuron whom to connect to. This essay argues that comparing the full wiring diagram with where cell-adhesion proteins are expressed could crack that code.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Topics in Developmental Biology (2016), Scott Emmons frames the connectome as the last major undescribed piece of neuroanatomical phenotype. He recounts 15 years of work culminating in the 1986 hermaphrodite map (118 neuron classes, 302 neurons) and the 2012 PC-enabled reconstruction of male mating circuits (Jarrell et al.). Male posterior connectivity had exceeded 1970s paper accounting despite not being a size problem. The proposed solution is a combinatorial adhesion-protein code read out by aligning expression with the entire chemical-plus-gap-junction graph.
summaries.advanced: This is a perspective, not a gene-to-synapse lookup table. “Final frontier” is rhetorical. The 1986 map is hermaphrodite-only; male completeness is attributed to Jarrell et al. 2012. Claims about EM’s “tiny viewing window” are historical context, not a methods benchmark. No new connectivity counts are presented in the extract.

plain_language_summary: We still do not know which genes tell each worm neuron whom to connect to. This essay argues that comparing the full wiring diagram with where cell-adhesion proteins are expressed could crack that code.

ocar.opportunity: Array tomography can combine fluorescence and electron microscopy on serial sections, so molecular labels could be placed onto ultrastructure with high confidence—including electrical synapses that connectomics often under-annotates.
ocar.challenge: Correlating molecular labeling with ultrastructure remains difficult; registration of super-resolution light images to SEM on the same high-pressure-frozen section needed unbiased landmarks and workable protocols.
ocar.action: Markert, Britz, Proppert, Lang, Witvliet, Mulcahy, Sauer, Zhen, Bessereau, and Stigloher combine high-pressure freezing and freeze substitution with SEM plus structured illumination microscopy (SIM) and dSTORM on the same C. elegans sections (Neurophotonics, 2016).
ocar.resolution: They correlate EM and super-resolution data using endogenous cellular landmarks and freely available software, identify and label gap junctions with stated precision and confidence, and show that dSTORM (typical ~20 nm lateral resolution) can resolve distinct ventral-nerve-cord microtubules as fiducials. SIM was sufficient for their gap-junction analysis.
ocar.future_work: They argue the methods can extend to still smaller structures and toward a “functionally understood, truly complete connectome” that includes molecular identity of electrical synapses; dSTORM-level registration was not required for the gap-junction results shown.

summaries.beginner: Electrical synapses are tiny protein channels that are hard to name in electron-microscope pictures. This team images the same worm tissue with super-resolution light microscopy and electron microscopy so the channels can be both seen and molecularly labeled.
summaries.intermediate: In Neurophotonics (2016), Markert and colleagues add super-resolution array tomography to C. elegans connectomics. High-pressure freezing and freeze substitution preserve ultrastructure; the same sections are imaged by SEM and by SIM or dSTORM. Correlation uses endogenous landmarks rather than added fiducials. They demonstrate gap-junction identification and labeling, and show distinct microtubules in the ventral nerve cord in both EM and dSTORM (typical ~20 nm lateral resolution) as potential intrinsic fiducials. Gap-junction analysis in the study used SIM.
summaries.advanced: “Precision and confidence” for gap-junction calls is qualitative in the selected extract; no numeric registration error is given here. dSTORM microtubule fiducials are presented as enabling still finer localization, not as the method used for the main gap-junction dataset. Completeness of electrical-synapse census in a whole connectome is a stated goal, not a result of this paper.

plain_language_summary: Electrical synapses are tiny protein channels that are hard to name in electron-microscope pictures. This team images the same worm tissue with super-resolution light microscopy and electron microscopy so the channels can be both seen and molecularly labeled.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans uses gap junctions in virtually all cells, and a surprisingly large innexin gene family could explain diverse junction types in development and in the connectome.
ocar.challenge: Many cell types express multiple innexins, producing heteromeric and heterotypic channels and enough redundancy that single-gene knockdowns often yield limited developmental or behavioral phenotypes; which subunit combinations actually assemble is still poorly known.
ocar.action: Hall reviews innexin gap junctions in Developmental Neurobiology (2016, published 2017): general properties, expression patterns, and known roles in tissue development and the animal’s connectome, restricting the scope to intercellular channels rather than speculative hemichannel functions.
ocar.resolution: The genome encodes 25 innexin genes; virtually every cell type appears to express at least one, often several (citing Altun et al., 2009). Overlapping expression supports diverse junction types. The review organizes composition as homomeric, heterotypic, or heteromeric and notes little is yet known about which subunits dock.
ocar.future_work: Experimental evidence in C. elegans for innexin hemichannels (ATP release or organelle roles) is described as relatively little. Mapping which subunit combinations occur in identified connectome gap junctions remains open.

summaries.beginner: Worms do not use the same gap-junction proteins that we do; they use innexins. This review explains that worms have many innexin genes, most cells use more than one, and that redundancy makes single-gene knockouts surprisingly mild.
summaries.intermediate: In Developmental Neurobiology (received May 2016; volume year 2017), David Hall reviews C. elegans gap junctions as innexin channels, not connexins, with distant homology to vertebrate pannexins. The genome encodes 25 innexins, a larger family than in Drosophila or the planarian Dugesia as stated here. Expression is widespread and overlapping, which the review links to diverse junction types and to muted single-gene knockdown phenotypes. Scope is intercellular channels; hemichannel roles are noted as poorly evidenced in the worm. Figure 1 classifies homomeric, heterotypic, and heteromeric subunit arrangements.
summaries.advanced: This is a narrative review; the 25-gene count and “virtually every cell type” expression claim cite Altun et al. 2009 rather than new measurements. Which innexin combinations form identified electrical synapses in the connectome is largely unknown. Behavioral and developmental roles are surveyed, not re-demonstrated experimentally here.

plain_language_summary: Worms do not use the same gap-junction proteins that we do; they use innexins. This review explains that worms have many innexin genes, most cells use more than one, and that redundancy makes single-gene knockouts surprisingly mild.

ocar.opportunity: A complete census of macaque bipolar types and their type-specific synapses would show how photoreceptor signals are partitioned onto ganglion-cell pathways, including ON/OFF counterparts.
ocar.challenge: Twelve morphological bipolar types were already named from Golgi, EM, and immunohistochemistry, but type-specific contact numbers and ON versus OFF pairing in rod-dense perifovea still needed serial EM.
ocar.action: Tsukamoto and Omi use serial-section transmission EM in macaque perifovea (Frontiers in Neuroanatomy, 2016) to reconfirm ON cone bipolar classes IMB, DB4, DB5, DB6, GB, and BB and to quantify photoreceptor and ganglion-cell contacts.
ocar.resolution: They pair ON types with OFF counterparts (IMB and BB with FMB; DB4 with DB2; DB5 with DB3a; DB6 with DB1; GB with DB3b). DB6 directs 70% of ribbon contacts to ON midget ganglion cells (OFF DB1: 60% to OFF MG). GB contacts rods and cones, paralleling OFF DB3b, a circuit they link to fast mesopic rod signals. Two-step synapses largely restrict S-cone output to small bistratified and some OFF midget ganglion cells.
ocar.future_work: Axon-terminal statistics in Figure 10 are means ± SD on small n (GB n=2; thirty terminals total). ON versus OFF identity is receptor type (mGluR6 vs AMPA/kainate), not invaginating versus basal contact; basal-contact percentages vary with eccentricity.

summaries.beginner: In the monkey retina, bipolar cells sort cone and rod signals toward different ganglion cells. This electron-microscopy study lists how each ON bipolar type connects and matches it to an OFF partner.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neuroanatomy (2016), Tsukamoto and Omi reconstruct ON bipolar connectivity in rod-dense macaque perifovea with SSTEM. They reconfirm IMB, DB4, DB5, DB6, GB, and BB, and report type-specific synapses: DB4 reciprocal contacts with an ON-OFF lateral amacrine (like OFF DB2); GB mixed rod–cone contacts (like OFF DB3b); DB6 70% of ribbon outputs to ON midget ganglion cells (OFF DB1 60% to OFF MG). IMB contacts M/L- but not S-cones; BB does the reverse, yet a single-S-cone BB resembles IMB morphologically. S-cone signals are largely funneled to small bistratified ganglion cells and some OFF midget cells.
summaries.advanced: Contact percentages (e.g., 70%, 60%, basal-contact 38/52/66% for DB5/DB4/DB6 on perifoveal M/L cones with about 31 ribbons at 3 mm) are from this perifoveal sample and are discussed as intermediate between foveal and peripheral literature. Figure 10 n is small, especially GB (2 cells). Catalog dataset tags mention mouse retina; the paper is macaque. ON/OFF is defined by glutamate receptor, not by invaginating versus basal ultrastructure.

plain_language_summary: In the monkey retina, bipolar cells sort cone and rod signals toward different ganglion cells. This electron-microscopy study lists how each ON bipolar type connects and matches it to an OFF partner.

ocar.opportunity: X-rays can image thick samples without serial sectioning, offering a faster path to millimeter-scale 3D brain maps at mesoscale resolution that could complement light and electron connectomics.
ocar.challenge: Conventional photon or electron pipelines require thin slicing, staining, and stitching (the authors cite ~1,000 hours to stitch BigBrain at 20 µm and ~three months to image 1 mm³ by EM at 20 nm with ~30 nm slices).
ocar.action: Dyer, Gray Roncal, Fernandes, Gürsoy, De Andrade, Fezzaa, Xiao, Vogelstein, Jacobsen, Körding, Kasthuri and colleagues demonstrate synchrotron X-ray microtomography (µCT) of mouse brain and a pipeline for preparation, imaging, automated segmentation of cells, vessels, and myelinated axons, plus statistical analysis (eNeuro / arXiv 2016).
ocar.resolution: They produce mesoscale maps at about 1 µm³ resolution from millimeter-scale volumes and argue that µCT enables rapid quantification of large brain volumes as a complement to other mapping efforts. Processing was scaled on LONI with NeuroData storage of chunked, padded blocks.
ocar.future_work: This is mesoscale architecture (cells, vessels, myelin), not synaptic connectivity. Segmentation and density estimation (k-nearest neighbor style, k=√N) are pipeline components whose biological error rates are not fully specified in the selected extract.

summaries.beginner: Cutting a brain into thousands of slices to photograph it is slow. This team uses synchrotron X-rays to scan thick pieces of mouse brain in 3D and automatically counts cells and blood vessels.
summaries.intermediate: In work published as eNeuro (DOI 10.1523/eneuro.0195-17.2017; selected extract is arXiv:1604.03629v2, 2016), Dyer and colleagues use synchrotron µCT to image millimeter-scale mouse-brain volumes at ~1 µm³ resolution without sectioning. They integrate sample preparation, reconstruction, and automated segmentation of cells, blood vessels, and myelinated axons, then statistical density analysis. Motivating contrasts include BigBrain stitching (~1,000 hours at 20 µm) and EM (~three months per mm³ at 20 nm). Large-scale runs used LONI and NeuroData with padded chunks to reduce edge effects.
summaries.advanced: The extract is the arXiv preprint; catalog authors include Judy A. Prasad, who is not on this author list. Resolution is mesoscale, not synapse-level. Timing comparisons (BigBrain, EM) are cited as motivation, not head-to-head experiments in this study. Automated cell counts depend on processing parameters (grid, k=√N) described in the methods excerpt.

plain_language_summary: Cutting a brain into thousands of slices to photograph it is slow. This team uses synchrotron X-rays to scan thick pieces of mouse brain in 3D and automatically counts cells and blood vessels.

ocar.opportunity: Direction selectivity in starburst amacrine cell dendrites is a model computation where connectomic wiring, a constrained network model, and calcium imaging can be combined across species.
ocar.challenge: How much SAC direction selectivity comes from intrinsic properties versus network connectivity was unclear, and mouse versus rabbit inhibitory wiring had not been compared at synapse-distribution resolution.
ocar.action: Ding, Smith, Poleg-Polsky, Diamond, and Briggman reconstruct SAC circuitry in mouse retina, build an anatomically constrained SAC network model, and test predictions with dendritic calcium imaging (Nature, 2016).
ocar.resolution: They report two previously unknown mouse features: input and output synapses are segregated, with inputs restricted to proximal dendrites; and inhibitory-input distribution differs from rabbit. The model indicates that this wiring supports lower linear-velocity tuning matching smaller eye diameter, conserving angular-velocity tuning, and that inhibition extends contrast range and alters receptive-field structure. Imaging confirmed the directional predictions.
ocar.future_work: Simulations underrepresented SAC–SAC convergence (cells receive input from dozens of neighbors) and omitted wide- and narrow-field amacrine inputs and detailed bipolar circuitry. Stimulus features such as size and spatial frequency remain unexplored. Sample size was not predetermined; all n are biological replicates. Tissue was P30 C57BL/6.

summaries.beginner: Some retinal cells fire more when a bar moves one way than the other. This study maps mouse starburst-cell wiring, finds it differs from rabbit, and shows the difference may keep angular speed tuning similar despite different eye sizes.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature (2016), Ding and colleagues present a mouse-retina connectomic reconstruction of starburst amacrine cell (SAC) circuitry. Input synapses are confined to proximal dendrites and separated from outputs; inhibitory SAC–SAC wiring differs from rabbit. An anatomically constrained model predicts that mouse connectivity encodes lower linear velocities, compensating for smaller eye diameter and conserving angular-velocity tuning, and that proximal inhibition extends contrast tuning and changes receptive-field structure. Calcium imaging of mouse SAC dendrites confirmed directional predictions. The discussion treats proximal-versus-distal input location as a computationally consequential detail.
summaries.advanced: Mouse–rabbit comparison depends on prior rabbit anatomy as well as this mouse reconstruction. The model omits many SAC inputs and bipolar detail; the authors say it guided physiology but underrepresented connectivity. No sample-size calculation. Catalog stages include “infrastructure”; the paper is retina circuit/connectomics. Extract is the NIH author manuscript.

plain_language_summary: Some retinal cells fire more when a bar moves one way than the other. This study maps mouse starburst-cell wiring, finds it differs from rabbit, and shows the difference may keep angular speed tuning similar despite different eye sizes.

ocar.opportunity: Experimentally mapping numbers, locations, and probabilities of all synaptic connection types in even a small neocortical volume is still intractable, so an algorithm that predicts a microcircuit connectome from sparse data could accelerate mapping.
ocar.challenge: Six cortical layers contain thousands of unique connection types between neuron types, of which only a handful have been measured; axo-dendritic appositions far outnumber true synapses.
ocar.action: Reimann, King, Muller, Ramaswamy, and Markram present a data-driven pruning algorithm in Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience (2015) that yields three parameters per connection type to predict biologically viable synaptic anatomy in a somatosensory microcircuit.
ocar.resolution: After filtering appositions onto biologically plausible compartments, a three-step prune (modified from Fares and Stepanyants, 2009) converts potential synapses into a predicted connectome. For 38 experimentally characterized pathways they match measured mean and SD of synapses per connection; for 2987 other pathways they predict those statistics from apposition counts. Predictions reproduce experimental connectivity data not used by the algorithm.
ocar.future_work: When all extra-microcircuit afferents are included, dendritic synapse density could add a constraint. Incorrect neuronal composition or morphologies will make predictions fail, which the authors treat as a test of the input data. Structural-plasticity pools of unused multi-synaptic connections are reserved, not functionally validated here.

summaries.beginner: Nobody can measure every synapse type in a piece of cortex. This team writes a computer recipe that starts from near-touches between axons and dendrites and prunes them down to a predicted wiring diagram, then checks it against the few types that have been measured.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience (2015), Reimann and colleagues (Blue Brain Project) digitally reconstruct the micro-scale connectome of a neocortical microcircuit by enforcing established connectivity principles. Potential synapses are axo-dendritic, axo-somatic, and axo-axonic appositions filtered by compartment (e.g., chandelier cells onto axon initial segments). A three-parameter pruning algorithm is fit to 38 experimentally characterized pathways using mean and SD of synapses per connection, and applied to 2987 other pathways using predicted means from apposition counts (with a generalized CV of 0.32). Bouton-density × axon-length further constrains parameters. Held-out experimental connectivity is reported as reproduced.
summaries.advanced: This is an in silico prediction, not an EM-mapped cortical connectome. The 0.25 transition-width value is chosen so single-synapse connections are <1%, a modeling choice. Most pathways (2987) lack direct measurements; their synapse-per-connection statistics are themselves predicted. Success depends on morphology and composition data being correct. Plasticity pruning randomly removes whole connections independently of synapse number.

plain_language_summary: Nobody can measure every synapse type in a piece of cortex. This team writes a computer recipe that starts from near-touches between axons and dendrites and prunes them down to a predicted wiring diagram, then checks it against the few types that have been measured.

ocar.opportunity: Membrane-detection probability maps from pixel-wise classifiers are a standard first step toward EM neurite segmentation; a learned iterative refiner could close gaps and suppress false membranes without a separate graphical merge model.
ocar.challenge: Isolated per-pixel membrane probabilities leave gaps that merge neurites and false membranes that split them—errors that destroy circuit reconstruction even when pixel error looks acceptable.
ocar.action: Wu trains a convolutional network (I-CNN) on arXiv (2015) to recover the masked center-pixel label of patches from a membrane-detection probability map, then applies the net iteratively over the map.
ocar.resolution: Iterating on MDPMs substantially reduces foreground-restricted Rand error for the first several rounds (about six before the gain disappears and then deteriorates). On the ISBI 2012 test stack after six rounds, reported Rand error is 0.0263 versus 0.0551 from the original CNN map. Pixel and warping errors drop on the first round then partly rebound.
ocar.future_work: Pixel-wise application is computationally redundant; the author proposes converting to a fully convolutional form and injecting noise at the center instead of a fixed mask. Extending to 3D context is described as straightforward but more training-data hungry.

summaries.beginner: A first-pass computer map of cell membranes in electron-microscope pictures is often gappy. This paper trains a second network to fill in missing membrane from the neighborhood and runs it several times, which improves how well neurons stay separated.
summaries.intermediate: On arXiv (2015), Xundong Wu introduces an iterative CNN that refines membrane-detection probability maps (MDPMs) by predicting a held-out center pixel from surrounding MDPM patches. No superpixel or CRF merge step is used. On ISBI 2012, six refinement rounds yield Rand error 0.0263 versus 0.0551 for the unrefined CNN map. Rand-error improvement fades after about six iterations; pixel and warping errors improve first then reverse. The method is motivated by 12 TB-scale mouse V1 ssTEM (4×4×45 nm) as a manual-segmentation bottleneck.
summaries.advanced: The 0.0263 Rand error is a challenge-board number from a specific starting MDPM (Ciresan-style), not a claim to have beaten every contemporaneous entry on all metrics. Iteration count is a hyperparameter; too many rounds hurt. The extract does not include Table 1’s full metric set. This is 2D membrane refinement, not 3D instance reconstruction.

plain_language_summary: A first-pass computer map of cell membranes in electron-microscope pictures is often gappy. This paper trains a second network to fill in missing membrane from the neighborhood and runs it several times, which improves how well neurons stay separated.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans has a fully mapped directed connectome plus extensive behavioral and physiological data, so flow-based analysis could link network structure to multi-scale signal propagation without pre-assigning cell classes.
ocar.challenge: Relating dense synaptic architecture to functional dynamics is still hard; static graph statistics may miss directed, multi-resolution flow.
ocar.action: Bacik, Schaub, Beguerisse-Díaz, Billeh, and Barahona analyze flow propagation on the directed C. elegans neuronal network in PLoS Computational Biology (2015; arXiv extract dated 2016).
ocar.resolution: They report flow-based groupings at several granularities related to functional and anatomical constituents; in silico single- and double-neuron ablations that most disrupt multi-resolution flow structure, proposed as candidates for in vivo tests; and four flow roles from incoming versus outgoing flow patterns, interpreted in input–response terms.
ocar.future_work: The selected extract is mostly front matter and references; ablation rankings and role assignments should be read from the full figures. Flow on the binary/weighted directed graph is not a biophysical simulation of voltage or neuromodulation.

summaries.beginner: This paper treats the worm’s directed wiring diagram like a traffic network. It groups neurons by how signals would flow, predicts which cell deletions would scramble that flow, and sorts cells into four flow roles.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Computational Biology (2015), Bacik and colleagues apply multi-resolution flow analysis to the C. elegans directed connectome. They obtain flow-based communities they relate to known anatomy and function, scan all single and double node deletions for disruption of that multi-scale flow, and cluster neurons by directional in- versus out-flow profiles into four roles without imposing sensory/inter/motor labels a priori. The author summary frames the work as integrating single-neuron knowledge into a network-level picture of operation.
summaries.advanced: The supplied PDF extract does not include the results figures or ablation tables; quantitative rankings are therefore not restated here. Flow communities depend on the Markov-time / map-equation style methods cited in the bibliography. In silico ablation is topological, not a substitute for laser ablation physiology. Catalog dataset is the White-era connectome lineage; exact edge-weighting conventions should be checked in the full methods.

plain_language_summary: This paper treats the worm’s directed wiring diagram like a traffic network. It groups neurons by how signals would flow, predicts which cell deletions would scramble that flow, and sorts cells into four flow roles.

ocar.opportunity: White et al. (1986) published the first complete synaptic wiring diagram of an animal and thereby founded connectomics as a practical research program.
ocar.challenge: Whether that hermaphrodite map would generalize, whether C. elegans is ancestral or highly derived, and how to turn a connectome plus other data into an understanding of brain function remained open 26 years later.
ocar.action: Emmons writes a Philosophical Transactions commentary (2015) for the journal’s 350th anniversary, recounting how Brenner’s manuscript arrived at the Royal Society in 1984 as six notebooks nicknamed “The mind of a worm.”
ocar.resolution: He treats the 1986 paper as a foundational resource that stimulated C. elegans biology across fields, notes that more powerful computers enabled new connectomes after a 26-year gap, and analogizes a connectome to a genome: not every answer, but the basis for asking the right functional questions.
ocar.future_work: He asks how fly (~100,000 neurons) or human (stated as 10^8 times larger than C. elegans) connectivity will compare, and whether the worm’s relatively simple, fixed structure is a relevant model or a derived special case.

summaries.beginner: This commentary retells how the first complete wiring diagram of an animal—the worm C. elegans—was published in 1986 and why that map still shapes neuroscience.
summaries.intermediate: In Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B (2015), Scott Emmons comments on White et al. (1986), “The structure of the nervous system of the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans.” He describes the August 1984 submission of a huge manuscript in six notebooks, Brenner’s cover letter, and the project’s origin in applying genetics to the brain using a 1 mm worm with only 1000 cells. The wiring diagram was in hand by 1984. The piece was written for the journal’s 350th anniversary and emphasizes the 26-year wait until computing made similar maps feasible again.
summaries.advanced: This is historical commentary, not a reanalysis of synapses. The “1000 cells” figure is whole-animal cell number, not neuron number. The human-brain size comparison (“10^8 times larger”) is the author’s order-of-magnitude statement. Anecdotes draw on literature and Royal Society materials plus personal communications listed in acknowledgements.

plain_language_summary: This commentary retells how the first complete wiring diagram of an animal—the worm C. elegans—was published in 1986 and why that map still shapes neuroscience.

ocar.opportunity: Brain disease rarely stays at one locus; axonal pathways constrain how perturbations spread, so a network-science view of the connectome could explain neuropathology and generate predictions.
ocar.challenge: It is unclear how topology shapes responses to damage—maladaptive processes versus resources that allow adaptation—and how to move from description to predictive models of spread and functional consequence.
ocar.action: Fornito, Zalesky, and Breakspear, as described in the catalog abstract, review in Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2015) how brain-network topology shapes neural responses to damage.
ocar.resolution: They highlight maladaptive processes (diaschisis, transneuronal degeneration, dedifferentiation) and adaptive resources and processes (degeneracy, reserve, compensation), arguing that knowledge of network topology can support predictive models of disease spread and functional impact.
ocar.future_work: The catalog abstract presents this as a conceptual program for connectomic neuropathology; specific disease models and datasets are not extractable from the mismatched PDF.

summaries.beginner: Brain diseases often spread along the brain’s wiring rather than staying in one spot. This review argues that mapping those networks helps explain how damage travels and how the brain sometimes copes.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2015), Fornito, Zalesky, and Breakspear consider the connectome as the substrate that constrains pathological spread. According to the catalog abstract, they review how topology shapes responses to damage, covering maladaptive processes such as diaschisis, transneuronal degeneration, and dedifferentiation, and adaptive resources including degeneracy and reserve plus compensation. They argue that a network-science approach is integral to neuropathology and can yield predictive models of spread and functional consequences.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Mansour et al., Neuroimage: Reports (2026), “The damaged connectome: Mechanisms and consequences of brain network reorganization following neurotrauma,” a TBI narrative review, not Fornito et al. 2015. Numbers and claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract. Do not treat the 2026 TBI review’s clinical or imaging discussion as part of this work.

plain_language_summary: Brain diseases often spread along the brain’s wiring rather than staying in one spot. This review argues that mapping those networks helps explain how damage travels and how the brain sometimes copes.

ocar.opportunity: Invasive axonal tracing in animals yields weighted macroscale connectome maps; the open BAMS-II rat projection database lets topology be studied with connection strength, not only binary edges.
ocar.challenge: Prior mammalian connectome studies showed small-world, modular, and rich-club structure, but whether pathways with different topological roles systematically differ in projection strength was unclear.
ocar.action: van den Heuvel, Scholtens, and de Reus analyze BAMS-II pathways among 67 cortical and subcortical rat regions in Brain Structure and Function (2015).
ocar.resolution: They confirm small-world, modular, and rich-club organization. Intramodular connections are stronger than intermodular ones; hub-to-hub rich-club pathways are stronger than peripheral–peripheral edges. Different weight classes show different topological structure, suggesting varying roles and origins of pathways.
ocar.future_work: They call for work on whether weak versus strong pathways differ in macroscale neuroarchitectonics and on the hypothesized high vulnerability of high-degree regions and their connections in disease.

summaries.beginner: This paper treats the rat brain as a network of 67 regions linked by traced axons of different strengths. Strong links tend to sit inside modules and between hub regions, not just anywhere.
summaries.intermediate: In Brain Structure and Function (2015; volume 2016), van den Heuvel, Scholtens, and de Reus analyze the rat macroscale connectome from the BAMS-II axonal-projection database (67 cortical and subcortical regions). Network analysis confirms small-world, modular, and rich-club organization consistent with other mammals. Extending those observations, they show topological role covaries with strength: intramodular edges are stronger than intermodular edges, and rich-club hub-to-hub pathways are stronger than connections among peripheral nodes. Weight-stratified subgraphs differ in topology.
summaries.advanced: This is a weighted graph of tracer-defined regional pathways, not a synaptic micro-connectome. Strength values inherit BAMS-II scoring conventions and missing-projection uncertainty. Catalog stages include proofreading/infrastructure; the paper is macroscale graph analysis. Disease-vulnerability remarks in the discussion are hypotheses citing human-hub literature, not rat lesion data in this extract.

plain_language_summary: This paper treats the rat brain as a network of 67 regions linked by traced axons of different strengths. Strong links tend to sit inside modules and between hub regions, not just anywhere.

ocar.opportunity: Automatic EM segmentation still needs costly proofreading and exhaustive pixel ground truth; training that uses sparse labels and favors correctable errors would reduce human time in reconstruction.
ocar.challenge: False merges (under-segmentation) are harder to fix than false splits, yet many computer-vision metrics treat them symmetrically; full pixel annotations are expensive, and appearance shifts across large brains may require many predictors.
ocar.action: Parag (arXiv, 2015, HHMI Janelia) proposes an active-learning training scheme with sparse labeling of pixels and superpixel boundaries, prioritizing minimization of false merges over false splits.
ocar.resolution: Experiments on 2D and 3D data are reported to yield segmentations more amenable to neural reconstruction than existing methods. Label propagation and random-forest classifiers are shown as complementary on early query samples (cytoplasm, membrane, mitochondria).
ocar.future_work: The author expects appearance to vary across large brain regions, so efficient retraining will matter. Extension to other superpixel-aggregation domains (light-microscopy cell tracking, blood-cell segmentation) is suggested. Minimal under-segmentation is treated as a prerequisite for skeleton-constrained reconstruction methods such as Helmstaedter et al. 2013.

summaries.beginner: Computers that color in neurons on electron-microscope pictures still make mistakes, and gluing two cells together is worse than accidentally cutting one. This paper trains the computer with a few clicks and tries extra hard not to glue cells together.
summaries.intermediate: On arXiv (2015), Toufiq Parag argues that EM segmentation should be judged by proofreading labor, not only Rand error or variation of information. He trains classifiers with active learning and sparse labels on pixels and superpixel boundaries instead of exhaustive pixel ground truth, with an explicit bias against false merges. 2D and 3D experiments are described as producing outputs easier to reconstruct. A figure compares label propagation versus random forest on the first queried samples for cytoplasm, membrane, and mitochondria, including cases each method uniquely gets right.
summaries.advanced: No numeric error table is in the selected extract, so “more amenable” is the author’s summary of experiments, not a restated leaderboard. The merge-versus-split priority is a design choice aligned with connectomic proofreading, not a universal computer-vision optimum. Generalization across brain regions is anticipated, not demonstrated at whole-brain scale here.

plain_language_summary: Computers that color in neurons on electron-microscope pictures still make mistakes, and gluing two cells together is worse than accidentally cutting one. This paper trains the computer with a few clicks and tries extra hard not to glue cells together.

ocar.opportunity: High-throughput EM produces petavoxel streams that neuroscientists need to explore interactively, including incomplete data still being acquired and overlaid high-resolution voxel segmentation.
ocar.challenge: GPU memory, preprocessing of full multiresolution hierarchies, and algorithms that assume complete volumes fail when data stream for months or years; a 1 mm³ EM volume is cited as ~1 Pbyte, with scanning at ~10 Mpixels/s taking several years.
ocar.action: Beyer, Hadwiger, Al-Awami, Jeong, Kasthuri, Lichtman, and Pfister present in IEEE Computer Graphics and Applications (2013) a visualization-driven system with multiresolution virtual memory that restricts computation to the visible subset and supports incomplete streams.
ocar.resolution: The system concurrently handles multiple volumes and high-resolution segmentation. Researchers used it on a 1-teravoxel mouse-cortex volume in which several hundred axons and dendrites and synapses had been segmented and labeled. Virtual memory allows direct access to a requested resolution without traversing an entire octree path on the GPU.
ocar.future_work: The extract focuses on rendering architecture versus prior octree and streaming systems; it does not claim automatic reconstruction. Display-aware streaming still depends on acquisition continuing in the background.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope brain pictures can be so large they will not fit in a graphics card. This team builds a viewer that only loads the piece you are looking at, even while the microscope is still scanning.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE Computer Graphics and Applications (2013), Beyer and colleagues describe petascale volume visualization for high-throughput EM. Design goals include interactive rates, concurrent volumes, overlay of voxel segmentation, and incomplete data. Motivating numbers: 25–50 nm slices at 3–5 nm pixels; 1 mm³ ~1 Pbyte; ~10 Mpixels/s implying years of scanning. The deployed example is a 1-teravoxel mouse-cortex volume with several hundred labeled axons, dendrites, and synapses. A multiresolution virtual-memory scheme avoids GPU octree-path traversal required by systems such as GigaVoxels.
summaries.advanced: This is a visualization systems paper, not a new connectome. “Several hundred” neurites is a usage report, not a completeness metric. Comparisons to ViSUS, GigaVoxels, and supercomputer in-situ rendering are architectural. Catalog dimension is segmentation; the contribution is interactive exploration of EM and segmentation overlays.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope brain pictures can be so large they will not fit in a graphics card. This team builds a viewer that only loads the piece you are looking at, even while the microscope is still scanning.

ocar.opportunity: GRASP can mark synapses by reconstituting split GFP across partners at light-microscopic resolution, which would accelerate mammalian circuit mapping if the method could be retargeted to mammalian synapses.
ocar.challenge: Prior GRASP in nematode and fly required substantial redesign for mammalian brains: fragments must traffic to synaptic membranes and reconstitute in vivo without the original carriers.
ocar.action: Kim, Zhao, Petralia, Yu, Peng, Myers, and Magee engineer mammalian GRASP (mGRASP) with chimeric synaptic split-GFP carriers designed in silico, then combine it with computational 3D neuron reconstruction (Nature Methods, 2011/2012).
ocar.resolution: Chimeric fragments were efficiently delivered to synaptic locations and reconstituted GFP fluorescence in vivo. Applied to long-range and local circuits in mouse hippocampus and thalamocortical regions, mGRASP supported analysis of synaptic distribution on single neurons and dendritic compartments. EM experiments (Petralia) are listed among author contributions for validation.
ocar.future_work: Different brain areas and synapse types may need tailored carriers and analysis. The authors position mGRASP as complementary to EM, optogenetics, Brainbow, trans-synaptic tracers, and array tomography, each of which they briefly critique. Additional validation remains advised.

summaries.beginner: A trick from worms and flies makes a green glow only where two neurons actually touch at a synapse. This team redesigns that trick for mouse brains and uses it to map connections in hippocampus and thalamus-to-cortex pathways.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Methods (2011; journal issue 2012), Kim and colleagues introduce mGRASP: split-GFP fragments optimized with mammalian synaptic transmembrane carriers via in silico protein design. Reconstituted fluorescence reports synapse location at light-microscopic resolution. Combined with stitching, tracing, and puncta-detection software, they map synapses in mouse hippocampal and thalamocortical circuits at single-neuron and dendritic-compartment resolution. GenBank accessions for Cre-dependent and Cre-independent rAAV vectors and pre-/post-mGRASP fusions are provided. Author contributions assign EM to Petralia.
summaries.advanced: Light-microscopic reconstituted GFP is a proximity/complement reporter, not a full ultrastructural synapse catalog; EM is used for validation, not whole-circuit EM reconstruction. Axon–dendrite overlap alone is explicitly insufficient, which motivates mGRASP. Area-specific optimization is flagged as future work. Catalog organism/dataset tags (fly, C. elegans) reflect GRASP’s history; this paper is mammalian.

plain_language_summary: A trick from worms and flies makes a green glow only where two neurons actually touch at a synapse. This team redesigns that trick for mouse brains and uses it to map connections in hippocampus and thalamus-to-cortex pathways.

ocar.opportunity: Complete network maps need synaptic resolution, coverage of a canonical region, and neuronal classification; TEM can provide the first two if mosaicking, registration, classification, and browsing can be scaled.
ocar.challenge: Building large ssTEM volumes requires mosaicking distorted tiles and registering distorted mosaics; most molecular class markers are poorly compatible with optimal TEM; user-guided tools cannot keep up with canonical-field scale.
ocar.action: Anderson, Jones, Yang, Shaw, Watt, Koshevoy, Spaltenstein, Jurrus, Kannan, Whitaker, Mastronarde, Tasdizen, and Marc present in PLoS Biology (2009) a framework combining TEM-compliant small-molecule profiling (CMP), SerialEM acquisition, ir-tools mosaicking/registration, and viewers (MosaicBuilder, Viking).
ocar.resolution: They embed classification maps into ssTEM volumes and manage terabyte-scale data. In well-posed tasks such as retinal complete-network mapping, volumes that would have taken decades can be assembled in months. One microscope captures 3,000 tiles/day; example inner-plexiform volumes use mosaics of 950–1,100 tiles across >400 sections. The stack can be parallelized across labs, including legacy film.
ocar.future_work: Automated synapse and gap-junction recognition is described as early-stage; analysis still relies on human tagging. They propose multi-TEM packetized acquisition into a central volume build and community annotation analogous to Galaxy Zoo.

summaries.beginner: Stitching thousands of electron-microscope snapshots into a 3D brain map used to take a career. This team releases software and a molecular-labeling strategy so large retinal wiring volumes can be built in months and browsed like a map.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Biology (2009), Anderson, Marc and colleagues describe an ultrastructural mapping framework: computational molecular phenotyping compatible with TEM, scripted SerialEM acquisition, automated mosaicking and slice-to-slice registration (ir-tools), and gigabyte-scale browsers (MosaicBuilder, Viking). They argue this removes three barriers—mosaicking, registration, viewing—and enables both new and legacy film datasets. For retinal complete-network mapping, terabyte volumes shift from decades to months. Throughput cited: 3,000 tiles/day on one high-performance TEM; inner-plexiform examples with 950–1,100 tiles per section over >400 sections.
summaries.advanced: “Months versus decades” is for well-posed canonical-field tasks, not arbitrary neuropil. Classification depends on CMP; without it, ssTEM reconstructions are described as of limited value. Synapse markup is still manual in this framework. Catalog lists many pipeline stages; the paper is infrastructure for ssTEM volume assembly plus molecular classification, not a finished whole-retina connectome in the extract.

plain_language_summary: Stitching thousands of electron-microscope snapshots into a 3D brain map used to take a career. This team releases software and a molecular-labeling strategy so large retinal wiring volumes can be built in months and browsed like a map.

ocar.opportunity: A physical map of neurons and their synapses is a necessary piece of understanding how circuits implement behavior and how they fail in disease.
ocar.challenge: Golgi impregnation, optical tract-tracing, and electron microscopy each have severe limits that make precise wiring diagrams hard to extract from histological images.
ocar.action: Lichtman, Livet, and Sanes review in Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2008) recent advances toward complete physical maps, including Brainbow-style multicolor labeling, and remaining obstacles.
ocar.resolution: They organize circuit-mapping strategies around single-cell staining, optically based tracing, and EM, then discuss new labeling and imaging opportunities. They coin “connectomes” by analogy to genomes and argue that unlike genomics, connectomics may need several labeling, imaging, reconstruction, and analysis methods in parallel.
ocar.future_work: Making difficult, labor-intensive steps mundane and automatic is presented as the path forward; the review surveys a subset of then-emerging approaches rather than delivering a mammalian wiring diagram.

summaries.beginner: This review explains why it is so hard to draw a precise wiring diagram of the brain from microscope pictures and surveys new coloring and imaging tricks, including rainbow-like neuron labels, that might help.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2008), Lichtman, Livet, and Sanes review anatomical strategies for circuit mapping: Golgi-style single-cell impregnation, optical tract-tracing, and electron microscopy, with their limitations. They outline what a complete physical map would need to sit alongside physiology and plasticity data, then discuss emerging methods aimed at that map. The conclusion compares connectomics to genomics: similarly demanding technically, but likely requiring multiple parallel approaches rather than one sequencing-like pipeline.
summaries.advanced: This is a short review/perspective (extract is the NIH author manuscript). It does not present new connectivity counts. “Technicolour” refers to multicolor genetic labeling (Brainbow lineage) as one of several approaches. Claims about C. elegans effort in related literature are not the focus here; the piece is about mammalian circuit-mapping obstacles circa 2008.

plain_language_summary: This review explains why it is so hard to draw a precise wiring diagram of the brain from microscope pictures and surveys new coloring and imaging tricks, including rainbow-like neuron labels, that might help.

ocar.opportunity: Electron microscopy is the only then-available method with resolution to follow every axon and dendrite in dense neuropil, so complete local wiring diagrams could again link function to anatomy.
ocar.challenge: Reconstructing even local circuits required serially sectioning and analyzing thousands of sections, a daunting manual bottleneck.
ocar.action: Briggman and Denk, as described in the catalog abstract, review in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2006) technological developments that improved volume-EM data quality and automated acquisition.
ocar.resolution: They argue that these developments open the prospect of reconstructing almost complete invertebrate and sizable fractions of vertebrate nervous systems, which could rekindle relating neural function to neuroanatomical circuitry.
ocar.future_work: The catalog abstract is a prospectus for volume EM; specific instrument comparisons are not taken from the mismatched PDF.

summaries.beginner: Following every wire in a piece of brain needs electron microscopy, but cutting and aligning thousands of slices used to be crushing work. This 2006 review says new automated 3D electron-microscope methods were starting to make large wiring diagrams realistic.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2006), Briggman and Denk review volume electron microscopy for neural circuit reconstruction. According to the catalog abstract, EM uniquely resolves dense neuropil, but large serial-section reconstructions had been inhibited by thousands of sections. They discuss then-recent improvements in volume-EM quality and automated acquisition, and they project reconstructions of almost complete invertebrate nervous systems and sizable vertebrate fractions as newly plausible.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Ströh et al., bioRxiv (2026), “Eyewire II – A connectomic resource for resolving cell types and circuits of the mouse retina” (DOI 10.64898/2026.05.28.727403), not Briggman and Denk 2006. Numbers and claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract. Do not treat Eyewire II’s ~1 mm² mouse-retina dataset or software table as part of this work.

plain_language_summary: Following every wire in a piece of brain needs electron microscopy, but cutting and aligning thousands of slices used to be crushing work. This 2006 review says new automated 3D electron-microscope methods were starting to make large wiring diagrams realistic.

ocar.opportunity: If multi-neuron modules with stereotyped function exist, they should appear as over-represented connectivity patterns (motifs) in a fully mapped wiring diagram, simplifying description of structure and function.
ocar.challenge: Unlike engineered electronics, evolution does not label its modules; infrequent but important motifs would be missed, and it is unclear what random-graph null models are appropriate.
ocar.action: Reigl, Alon, and Chklovskii search the C. elegans wiring diagram for recurring 2–5 neuron interconnectivity patterns, comparing counts to random-matrix ensembles that preserve smaller-pattern statistics (BMC Biology, 2004).
ocar.resolution: Some patterns of two, three, and four neurons—but not five—are significantly over-represented given the statistics of smaller patterns. Bidirectional doublets, several of 13 connected triplets, and several of 199 connected quadruplets are highlighted. These motifs are offered as candidate computational modules, possibly shared across species.
ocar.future_work: The algorithm ignores connections outside the N-node pattern (unless they create an N+1 motif). Multiplicity, spatial layout, and other factors are not in the binary adjacency matrix; the authors argue over-represented classes should remain so if later split into subclasses. Functions of motifs are not identified here.

summaries.beginner: The authors ask whether the worm’s wiring diagram contains small repeating circuit gadgets, like logic gates in electronics. They find some two-, three-, and four-cell patterns that show up more often than chance; five-cell patterns do not.
summaries.intermediate: In BMC Biology (2004), Reigl, Alon, and Chklovskii convert C. elegans connectivity to a binary adjacency matrix and count multi-neuron patterns against random ensembles that preserve smaller-scale statistics (e.g., degree and bidirectional edges). They report over-represented bidirectional doublets, several triplet classes, and several quadruplet classes, but not five-neuron patterns. Motifs are defined by internal connections only. The discussion contrasts this with clustering methods that group nodes by dense internal linkage, and notes the approach can be applied to incomplete maps though power grows with completeness.
summaries.advanced: “Chance” means a specified random-matrix null, not biological irrelevance. Binary Aij ignores synapse counts, gap versus chemical type, and extra-pattern inputs. Absence of five-node motifs is relative to that hierarchy of nulls. Candidate computational function is explicitly unverified. Wiring-diagram incompleteness of the early 2000s connectome is acknowledged as reducing statistical power.

plain_language_summary: The authors ask whether the worm’s wiring diagram contains small repeating circuit gadgets, like logic gates in electronics. They find some two-, three-, and four-cell patterns that show up more often than chance; five-cell patterns do not.

ocar.opportunity: Targeted grooming requires converting touch from a specific body site into a spatially matched motor action; a complete central map of fly-leg touch in the VNC plus cell-type genetics could reveal that transformation.
ocar.challenge: Vertebrate tactile circuits are complex and prior tracing was sparse, so how somatotopic maps drive spatially targeted grooming remained poorly understood even in insects.
ocar.action: Elabbady, Chou, Sustar, Cook, Collman, and Tuthill combine genetic tools and connectomics on bioRxiv (2026) to map Drosophila leg bristle axons in the ventral nerve cord and their downstream interneurons.
ocar.resolution: Bristle axons in the VNC follow the same cardinal axes as the developing leg. They target developmentally related local 23B interneurons with overlapping receptive fields of different shapes and sizes; those cells innervate distinct premotor pools that synapse onto leg motor neurons. Optogenetic activation of proximal-sensing (SS04746) versus distal-sensing (R21B10) 23B lines elicits spatially targeted grooming matching connectome-based fields.
ocar.future_work: The selected extract’s back half is supplemental figures and video legends rather than the main discussion; quantitative synapse fractions should be read from the full paper. Behavior is shown in headless flies with 5 Hz CsChrimson protocols.

summaries.beginner: A fly must scratch the exact spot that was touched. This preprint maps leg-touch neurons in the fly’s ventral nerve cord and shows a short chain of cells that turns a touch map into a well-aimed grooming movement.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (March 2026), Elabbady and colleagues describe a four-layer circuit for Drosophila leg grooming. Tactile bristles (one mechanosensory neuron each; sensitive to deflections less than 100 nm) send axons into the VNC in a somatotopic map aligned with developmental axes. Second-order 23B local interneurons tile that map with overlapping fields, then contact premotor interneurons that synapse on leg motor neurons. Optogenetic activation of proximal-sensing SS04746 versus distal-sensing R21B10 23B neurons produces region-specific grooming, consistent with connectomic receptive-field predictions. Supplemental analyses break 23B output onto premotor pools by leg neuropil (T1L, T1R, T2L).
summaries.advanced: The supplied extract jumps from the introduction to supplemental figure/video captions, so main-text statistics on cell counts and synapse fractions are not restated here. Optogenetic videos are 20 s trials in headless flies (5 s pre, 5 s 5 Hz laser, 10 s post). Catalog dataset tags point at FANC/MANC VNC resources; exact volume identity should be confirmed in the full methods. This is a preprint.

plain_language_summary: A fly must scratch the exact spot that was touched. This preprint maps leg-touch neurons in the fly’s ventral nerve cord and shows a short chain of cells that turns a touch map into a well-aimed grooming movement.

ocar.opportunity: Scientific annotation still spends most effort on the last mile of verification; imitating how experts navigate, click, and correct could use that process as training signal rather than only final labels.
ocar.challenge: Standard models map data to labels and discard expert interaction traces; it is unclear whether behavioral cloning of annotation skills transfers, scales, or encodes shared notions of error.
ocar.action: Chandok and Park introduce on arXiv (2026) a behavioral-cloning framework with 9 synthetic annotation tasks that simulate exploration, mistake correction, and strategy, then probe learned representations and fine-tune toward connectomics tracing.
ocar.resolution: Skills emerge hierarchically (GUI mechanics before task-critical decisions); models make fewer mistakes than the training traces yet can still correct errors. Larger models are more data-efficient in their scale range; multi-task pretraining enables fine-tuning while training from scratch fails. Linear probes decode task phase, progress, and a shared mistake representation (leave-one-task-out mean AUC 0.71 on 8/9 tasks). After fine-tuning, they report skeleton accuracy 95.1% on 28 held-out H01 axons versus 89.4% on 13 held-out C. elegans nerve-ring neurons.
ocar.future_work: They note BC inherits annotator biases; 3D EXPLORATION transfers poorly. Real-world scaling beyond synthetic tasks and two EM tracing GUIs remains the stated foundation, not a completed replacement for proofreading (they cite 33 person-years for a fly brain despite strong automation).

summaries.beginner: People who correct brain maps or animal videos spend most of their time clicking through software, not drawing from scratch. This paper trains computers to copy those click-by-click habits on toy tasks, then tries the same idea on tracing neurons.
summaries.intermediate: On arXiv (2026), Chandok and Park study behavioral cloning for scientific annotation using 9 synthetic tasks. They report hierarchical skill learning, improved data efficiency with model scale, successful multi-task pretraining versus failed from-scratch transfer, and linear probes that read out phase, object identity, progress, and errors (mistake-probe ROC AUC 0.87; correction 0.99 in one panel). PCA shows mistakes clustering across tasks. Fine-tuning on a shared tracing GUI is evaluated on 28 H01 axons and 13 C. elegans nerve-ring neurons (skeleton accuracy 95.1% vs 89.4%; placement@5 px 95.1% vs 78.0%). The introduction cites 33 person-years of fly-brain proofreading as motivation.
summaries.advanced: Primary benchmarks are synthetic; H01 and C. elegans numbers are a small held-out fine-tuning evaluation (28 and 13 processes). “Fewer mistakes than the training data” is a cloning result, not a claim of superhuman proofreading on production connectomes. 3D EXPLORATION is the transfer failure case. Impact-statement caveats include annotator bias and dual-use GUI agents. Catalog stages include proofreading; this is an imitation-learning study, not a released production proofreader.
