ocar.opportunity: Petascale synaptic maps such as MICrONS could supply biologically real connectivity constraints for artificial networks, testing whether cortical-column structure helps on standard vision tasks.
ocar.challenge: Emotion recognition from faces is hard (FER-2013 human-level accuracy cited as about 65±5%), and typical models use only loose biological metaphors rather than measured cortical wiring.
ocar.action: Prasanth and Tivnan present BioNIC on arXiv (2026): a feedforward net whose adjacency masks, laminar organization, and graded inhibition are taken from a single mouse V1 cortical column in MICrONS, plus Hebbian/homeostatic plasticity, LayerNorm, augmentation, synaptic noise, and convolutional front-end.
ocar.resolution: On FER-2013, BioNIC reaches 59.77±0.27% accuracy, described as comparable to a conventional baseline despite using only one column’s biologically relevant connections. Ablations remove inhibition, intra-layer connections, conv stages, noise, weight decay, augmentation, masks, lateral inhibition, LR scheduler, and label smoothing in turn.
ocar.future_work: Connectivity is limited to one cortical column. FER-2013 is not a neuroscience decoding task; success is computational plausibility of connectome-derived constraints, not a model of mouse vision. Several “biological” ingredients (LayerNorm, ReduceLROnPlateau, L2 weight decay, σ=0.06 noise) are ML counterparts of the authors’ analogies.

summaries.beginner: This paper builds an image classifier whose wiring is copied from a piece of mouse visual cortex mapped by the MICrONS project. It performs about as well as a normal neural net at guessing facial emotions, which the authors take as a sign that real brain wiring can guide AI design.
summaries.intermediate: On arXiv (January 2026; catalog venue Neurocomputing), Prasanth and Tivnan introduce BioNIC, constrained by MICrONS mouse V1 column connectivity (adjacency masks, laminar layout, graded inhibition) and trained with Hebbian updates plus homeostasis (α_hebb = α_home = 5×10^−4, f_target = 0.35), LayerNorm, data augmentation, and synaptic noise (σ=0.06). A convolutional stage is described as mimicking retinotopy. FER-2013 accuracy is 59.77±0.27%, compared with a matched conventional baseline and systematic ablations. Human-level FER-2013 accuracy is cited as about 65±5%.
summaries.advanced: Using V1 excitatory/inhibitory graphs to classify FER-2013 faces is a transfer of structure, not a claim that mouse V1 computes facial emotion. Accuracy near 60% is in the range of simple FER baselines, not state-of-the-art vision models. Hebbian terms are applied “instantaneously during training” alongside a standard classifier head (softmax). Catalog dataset DS13 MICrONS is the source of masks; evaluation is FER-2013. Extract is an arXiv PDF.

ocar.opportunity: How a nervous system wires itself from birth to adulthood is a core developmental question; temporal graph networks could model both lineage and changing synapses.
ocar.challenge: Static graphs miss developmental time; C. elegans uniquely offers lineage plus multiple EM connectomes across stages, but it is unclear whether temporal memory is required to predict lineage or classify connection stability.
ocar.action: Gayen and Alicea, as described in the catalog abstract, present DevoTG on arXiv (2026): Temporal Graph Neural Networks on a continuous-time lineage graph and a discrete-time connectome graph spanning eight EM reconstructions.
ocar.resolution: On lineage prediction the TGN reaches mean test AUC 0.839±0.007 (5 seeds; validation 0.937±0.001), 26 points above a static GNN with identical architecture (0.577±0.080). On the connectome they assign stable, developmental, and variable connection classes across 225 neurons and 858–2,496 connections from L1 to adult, and they track hub command interneurons AVA, AVB, and AVE.
ocar.future_work: The abstract presents DevoTG as open-source and extensible to other developing nervous systems; those claims are not verified from the mismatched PDF.

summaries.beginner: This paper, according to its abstract, uses time-aware graph networks to follow how the worm’s neurons are born and how their connections change from hatchling to adult, and it finds that remembering history beats a static network model.
summaries.intermediate: On arXiv (2026), Gayen and Alicea introduce DevoTG, applying Temporal Graph Neural Networks to C. elegans development. The catalog abstract describes a continuous-time dynamic graph of cell-division lineage and a discrete-time dynamic graph of the synaptic connectome across eight EM datasets. Lineage-task test AUC is 0.839±0.007 versus 0.577±0.080 for a static GNN. Connectome analysis yields three stability classes over 225 neurons and 858 to 2,496 connections from L1 birth to adult, with persistent centrality of AVA, AVB, and AVE. Interactive visualizations and a GitHub path (DevoLearn/DevoGraph) are advertised.
summaries.advanced: The PDF text supplied with pdf_trust=ok is Scherer et al., “Coherent Off-Policy Improvement of Large Behavior Models with Learned Rewards” (arXiv:2606.02194), a robotics imitation/IRL paper, not Gayen and Alicea DevoTG (arXiv:2606.21940). Numbers and claims above are taken only from the catalog abstract. Do not treat residual RL, CSIL, or π-0.5 manipulation-task success rates as part of this work.

ocar.opportunity: Continuous attractor models of head direction require fine-tuned symmetric weights, yet fly compass connectomes work despite heterogeneous wiring; reconciling those facts would generalize theory to biological circuits.
ocar.challenge: Small deviations from idealized symmetry should, in standard theory, destroy accurate integration, making biological attractors look implausible—yet they are robust.
ocar.action: Hulse, Aneesh, Romani, Jayaraman, and Hermundstad combine machine-learning search over attractor architectures with a construction algorithm that replaces each unit by output-preserving “dynamical clones,” then compare to multiple Drosophila connectomes (bioRxiv, 2026).
ocar.resolution: Clones embed hidden symmetries in heterogeneous connectivity, preserving ring-attractor dynamics and angular-velocity integration. Connectome analysis finds duplicated units whose wiring matches those hidden symmetries. RNNs with N=156 units are trained to integrate heading with Euler step Δt=0.01 s and τ=0.1 s, decoding heading from a linear readout of firing rates.
ocar.future_work: The outlook frames closed-loop iteration among ML discovery, theory, and connectome/physiology measurements. How much fine-tuning biology still needs, and how generally clone constructions apply beyond the fly compass, remain open.

summaries.beginner: Textbook models of the fly’s internal compass assume neatly symmetric wiring, but real connectomes look messy. This preprint shows how copying cells into “clones” can hide the needed symmetry inside messy weights so the compass still works.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (May 2026), Hulse and colleagues address ring-attractor dynamics in the Drosophila head-direction system. Machine-learning-optimized RNNs yield heterogeneous networks that still track heading. Inspired by those solutions, an algorithm replaces each canonical unit with multiple dynamical clones that preserve output weights, generating many functionally equivalent heterogeneous networks. Multiple fly connectomes show duplicated units consistent with hidden symmetries. Methods specify N=156 units, sigmoid rates, Δt=0.01 s, τ=0.1 s, and a 2-D linear readout on the unit circle.
summaries.advanced: Evidence for biological clones is connectomic similarity to the theory, not a developmental lineage proof in this extract. Training constraints on recurrent and velocity weights are varied (details “further below” in methods not fully in the extract). Catalog stages include preparation/infrastructure; the contribution is theory plus connectome-constrained comparison, not a new EM volume. This is a preprint.
